newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to set up financial policeman amid scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japan to set up financial policeman amid scandal.

text.p: Japan's Upper House of parliament on Monday passed a bill to set up a new government agency to police the scandal-hit financial sector, at a time when the country is headed for sweeping financial deregulation.

Under the new law, a fully independent agency will be set up under the Prime Minister's Office to inspect and supervise financial institutions, functions carried out in the past primarily by the powerful Ministry of Finance (MOF).

MOF, long viewed as Japan's most elite ministry, has been criticised for failing to uncover recent scandals involving suspected illegal dealings with racketeers by Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd, a leading Japanese bank, and top brokerage Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
The new agency will oversee all financial institutions and will have jurisdiction over Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission.

It will also be responsible for handling failures at financial institutions, although it would need to consult with the finance minister on any failure that could not be handled within the current framework and with the cabinet on any financial crisis.
More details regarding the agency will be decided by the end of August, when the ministries make their budget requests for the fiscal year starting in April 1998, government officials said.
The agency will be set up by July 1, 1998 and its chief will be hand-picked by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
MOF officials have said that the agency is likely to start with a staff of more than 300.
Analysts, while applauding the move, wondered whether the new supervisory body will be more effective than the old system, as most of its staff will be moving from the Finance Ministry.

"A new organisation will be set up, but the staff will be basically the same. We may end up just changing the packaging and sticking to the same system," said Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute Corp.
"I don't think they (MOF) gave up any power whatsoever," said Ron Bevacqua, an economist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.

In 1991, Hashimoto himself was forced to resign as finance minister after an earlier scandal at Nomura and other brokerages over compensation of favoured clients and ties to organised crime, as well as fraudulent loan schemes at some of the nation's top banks.
The ministry has also been under fire for its secretive handling of Japan's bad-loan crisis.
Public outrage flared last year over the use of 685 billion yen ($6.00 billion) in taxpayers' money to help liquidate failed "jusen" mortgage firms.

Analysts also pointed out that for government inspection to be more effective, it was necessary to coordinate with the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to avoid duplication of effort. The central bank will be given new powers by reforms in the decades-old BOJ law.

Other analysts doubted whether the new agency would get the funds and resources needed to check banks and brokerages properly, especially at a time when Japan is trying to get its public finances under control.

Under the forthcoming "Big Bang" financial reforms to liberalise Japanese markets, stiffer penalties and more stringent inspection will be essential to ensure order and credibility both at home and abroad, analysts say.
The government is expected to draft bills to strengthen the penalties for financial crimes and submit them to parliament as early as this autumn. ($1=114 yen)
